transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Thanks for seeing me. I'm... I'm a barber, actually. I've been doing it since I graduated, and I usually really love the job, you know? The whole atmosphere of the barbershop, talking to the guys, the precision of a good haircut. But I'm here because... well, it's the straight razors. Doing a hot towel shave or a crisp lineup is a huge part of the trade, people expect it, but I've gotten to the point where I will do almost anything to avoid using a straight razor at work. 

It's literally taking over my whole day. I'll constantly try to switch clients with the other barbers if I know a guy usually asks for a shave, or I'll just flat-out lie to the customer and say the blade is missing or that we're out of fresh ones. I've even caught myself hiding the razor in the very back of my station drawer under a bunch of towels just so I don't have to look at it or have it easily accessible. It's exhausting, constantly coming up with these schemes to get out of it. 

And the thing is, sometimes I just can't get out of it. If the shop is packed and my boss is right there watching, or a guy is already in the chair, I have to do it. And when I'm forced to, I am just shaking through the whole shave. I mean, my hands are trembling the entire time I'm holding that blade, and it's just... it's a nightmare. I can't keep doing my job like this, spending eight hours a day terrified of one of my own tools.
Is it just the straight razors that cause you this level of anxiety, or are there other things at work or in your daily life that make you feel similarly?

Honestly? No, it’s... it’s really just the straight razors. Which is the craziest part to me, because I know it’s just a tool. It’s a tool I trained with for hundreds of hours back when I graduated, you know? I can use clippers all day long. I can do a skin fade, I can use shears, thinning shears, trimmers, whatever—completely fine. I don't even think twice about them. 

But... but when that straight razor is just sitting there, open, on the rubber mat at my station... man, it’s like my brain just completely spirals. I just stare at the exposed blade and I get this intense, overwhelming feeling that I’m about to slip and just horribly hurt somebody. Or... or that I'm going to cut myself really badly. Like, I'll just picture the angle of the blade against a guy's neck, and I start thinking about how thin the skin is right there, and how incredibly sharp those disposable feather blades we use are... and my heart just drops into my stomach. 

It makes zero sense because I know the technique, I know how to stretch the skin, I know the exact stroke to use, but all I can focus on is the damage that little piece of metal could do. And it’s literally only that one specific tool! Everything else at work, everything else in my everyday life? Totally fine. I cook at home, I chop vegetables with massive chef's knives, no problem at all. But you put me in front of my own barber chair with a straight razor, and I just... I completely lose it.

Have you ever had an episode where you felt an intense fear or discomfort that reached a peak within minutes, with symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or trembling, in situations involving the straight razor?

Oh, God, yes. Yes, absolutely. It’s... it’s not even a slow build-up, you know? It’s completely instantaneous. Like, I could be having a totally great morning, just sweeping up hair around the chair from my last cut, joking with the other guys, feeling totally relaxed and in my element. But the literal second—and I mean the exact second—I hear a client sit down and ask for a razor shave, or even if I just accidentally glance down and see that the blade is flipped open on the mat... it just hits me like a freight train. 

My chest gets so incredibly tight, almost like someone is pulling a belt around my ribs and yanking it closed. And my hands instantly get clammy and sweaty, which, by the way, is the absolute worst thing when you're a barber because you need a firm, dry grip to do your job right, you know? But they just start sweating profusely. And it’s like my body has this automatic survival reaction where it just wants to physically back away from the station before my brain even has time to think about it. 

It all just peaks so unbelievably fast. Zero to a hundred in seconds. My heart will just start pounding out of my chest, racing so fast I can actually hear the blood rushing in my ears, and my hands will start doing that trembling thing I mentioned earlier. I’ll just be standing there, staring at the guy in the chair or staring at the open blade, and my legs will literally feel like they want to walk right out the front door of the shop. It's like a full-on physical panic taking over my entire body in the span of maybe ten seconds, just standing there paralyzed while the customer is waiting for me to lather him up.
Is your fear of the straight razor specifically about the harm it could cause to yourself or others, or is it also about something else?

No, it's... it's just the harm. That's the only thing. I mean, it's not like I'm afraid of the razor being dirty, or, I don't know, catching some kind of disease from it. We use barbicide for everything, and the blades are single-use anyway, so sanitation isn't even on my radar. And it's not like I'm worried about messing up the haircut or giving a bad shave and losing a client. I mean, I'm confident in my skills, I really am. I've been cutting hair for years, I know how to blend a fade, I know how to line up a beard. I know I'm a good barber.

It really, truly is just this overwhelming, paralyzing fear of the physical damage that specific blade can do. Like I said before, it's just this incredibly vivid image of the blade slipping. I'll just be standing there, looking at the guy's neck—you know, right where the jugular is, where the skin is so thin and delicate—and my brain just plays this awful, graphic movie of my hand jerking, or the client suddenly moving, and the blade just slicing right in. It's the blood, the injury, the thought of an ambulance having to come to the barbershop because I made one tiny mistake with my wrist. Or even just slicing my own thumb open while I'm trying to change the blade out. It's just the pure, physical danger of how sharp that exposed edge is. Nothing else. Just the blood and the injury.
Have you always had this fear of straight razors, or did it start at some point after you began working as a barber?

No, no, definitely not always. Like I said before, I trained with them for hundreds of hours back in school, so I used to be totally fine with them. I actually used to really enjoy the whole ritual of it, you know? The hot towel, the warm lather, the precision... it was almost like an art form to me. But this whole... this whole nightmare with the fear and the panic, it started about 11 months ago. 

Yeah, it’s been going on for almost a full year now, which just feels crazy to even say out loud. It all started right around the time my boss—the guy who owns the barbershop—decided to roll out this massive new promotion. He wanted to push this new "premium straight-razor shave package" to boost our ticket averages. And I mean, he was absolutely obsessed with it. He wanted every single barber pushing this package on every single guy who walked through the door, no matter what they originally came in for. 

And the thing is, we started having these huge, blow-out arguments over it. Because, you know, a proper straight-razor shave takes a lot of time. You can't just rush it. You need to prep the skin, you need to let the hot towel sit so the pores open up and the hair softens, you need to apply the pre-shave oil perfectly... but he was booking us back-to-back-to-back, trying to cram these premium packages into our standard thirty-minute time slots just to maximize profits. And I kept telling him, I was like, man, you cannot rush an exposed blade on a guy's neck! It's dangerous! We would just go back and forth, arguing in the breakroom, arguing before opening, just this constant, heavy tension about this shave package and the ridiculous time limits he was putting on us. 

And it was right in the middle of all those arguments, about 11 months ago, with all that pressure he was putting on me to just churn these shaves out like we were some kind of factory... that's when it happened. That's when I first looked down at the razor on my mat and just felt that absolute, paralyzing terror that I was going to slip because I was being forced to rush. And ever since those arguments over the package started, it's just been there. Every single day. It hasn't stopped once.
Is it the sight of the straight razor itself that triggers your fear, or is it more about the situation of having to use it on a client?

Well, it's... it's honestly both, but it really boils down to just the sight of the razor itself, especially when it's open. I mean, obviously, the situation of actually having to put it to someone's skin is terrifying, like I was saying before with the rushing and the pressure. But it doesn't even have to get that far for the panic to start. 

I know it’s just a tool. I really do know that logically. I mean, I trained with it for hundreds of hours, I passed my state boards with it, I know the mechanics of how it's supposed to work. And I can stand there and use clippers all day long, zero issues. I can use shears, thinning shears, edgers, whatever—totally fine. I can buzz a guy's head, I can do a complex skin fade with the foil shavers, and I don't feel an ounce of anxiety. 

But the literal second that straight razor is sitting open at my station... it's just game over. Even if it's just sitting there on the Barbicide mat, totally stationary, not even touching anybody. If the blade is exposed, if it's flipped open and I can see that incredibly sharp, thin edge gleaming under the shop lights, my brain just immediately goes to the absolute worst-case scenario. It just feels like I’m about to hurt somebody, or even cut myself badly, just by being near it. It's like the razor itself is radiating this intense, physical danger, just sitting there. I don't even have to be holding it. Just seeing it open, knowing how sharp it is and what it's capable of doing if one tiny thing goes wrong... that's all it takes. The sight of it alone just completely derails me.
Does your fear of straight razors occur when you're not at work, such as if you were to see one at home or in a store?

Well, the thing is, I don't really see them anywhere else, you know? Like, nobody really uses a straight razor at home unless they're super old-school or, I don't know, a hipster or something. I just use a regular cartridge razor at home for my own face. And you don't really see them in regular stores, either, mostly just specialty barber supply places, which I try to avoid going into now if I can help it. I just order my clipper guards and talc online so I don't have to walk past the display cases. 

But... but honestly, even just the thought of it, or if I'm at work and the situation comes up, the reaction is just instantaneous. It doesn't matter if it's sitting on my mat or if someone just mentions it. The second I hear a client ask for the premium razor shave package—like, if they just say the words—or if I see the blade flipped open on the counter, it's just immediate. My chest tightens up so fast it feels like someone pulled a strap around my ribs, and my hands get completely clammy and sweaty, which is the last thing you want when you're holding a sharp tool, right? Sweaty hands and a razor do not mix. 

And it's like my body just reacts before my brain even catches up. My feet literally want to step backward, away from the chair, away from the station, before I even consciously think about what's happening. It's this overwhelming physical urge to just get away from the blade, to back away from the danger. It's like a reflex. You know when you touch a hot stove and your hand jerks back before you even register the pain? It's exactly like that, but with my whole body, just trying to get away from that open blade the absolute second it's introduced into the situation.
Does your fear of straight razors ever occur when you're not at work or thinking about work?

Well, if I'm genuinely not at work, and I've actually managed to completely turn off my brain from thinking about the shop... no, no, it doesn't happen at all. Because, like I was saying before, you just don't really stumble across straight razors in the wild, you know? 

If I'm just hanging out at my apartment, or running errands, getting groceries, going to the gym, whatever... I'm totally fine. I actually try really, really hard to compartmentalize and just not think about work when I'm off the clock. I mean, when you're a barber, especially working for an owner who is constantly breathing down your neck about maximizing profits and pushing these premium packages, you kind of have to learn how to leave that stress at the door when you go home. Otherwise, it just eats you alive. 

So, like, if it's a Sunday or a Monday—those are my days off—and I'm just sitting on my couch watching football or playing Xbox or something, my mind is a million miles away from the barbershop. And in those moments, I feel completely, one hundred percent normal. My chest doesn't feel tight, I'm not sweating, nothing. It's really just strictly confined to that specific bubble of the shop, or if something forces me to picture the shop and that open blade. But if I'm just living my regular life outside of that and my mind is on other things? No, I don't get that panic at all. I mean, there's just no reason to, right? Because there aren't any exposed blades sitting around my living room waiting for me. It's really just the shop and the thought of the shop that does it.
If you were to see a straight razor in a non-work setting, such as at a friend's house or in a museum, would you experience the same level of fear or anxiety?

I mean... yeah, if I actually saw one? If I went to a buddy's house and he had one sitting out on his bathroom counter, or, like you said, if I was in a museum and there was some display of vintage grooming tools or whatever... yeah, I'm pretty sure I'd have the exact same reaction. 

Because it's not really about the barbershop itself, you know? It's the object. It's the blade. Even though the shop is where all the pressure is, where the boss is yelling and the clients are waiting, the actual fear... the physical panic... that's entirely centered on the razor. 

So if I'm at a friend's house, and I just go in to use the restroom, and I see one of those things flipped open next to the sink... man, just picturing it makes my stomach drop. Because the danger doesn't change just because the location changed, right? The blade is still just as sharp. It still has that same potential to just slice right through skin with zero effort. And my brain would just instantly go to that dark place. Like, what if I accidentally bump the counter and it falls? What if I try to catch it? What if someone else comes in and doesn't see it? 

It's just this immediate, overwhelming sense of threat. And honestly, it might even be a little bit worse in a weird way, because at least at the shop, I'm expecting to see them. I'm mentally prepared, or at least trying to be, to be in that environment. But if I'm just at a friend's place, having a beer, completely relaxed, and then suddenly—boom—there's an exposed straight razor? It would be like a jump scare. My heart rate would just spike through the roof, I'd start sweating, I'd probably have to just turn around and walk right out of the bathroom. I wouldn't even be able to wash my hands. I'd just need to get away from it immediately. So, yeah, the setting doesn't really matter if the blade is there. The blade is the problem.
Can you think of any situation outside of work where just thinking about a straight razor, without actually seeing one, would cause you to feel anxious or afraid?

Um... no, honestly, I really can't. Because, like I was trying to explain earlier, I just don't have any reason to think about them if I'm not at the shop or dealing with shop business. It's not like they just haunt my every waking moment for no reason, you know? 

Like, if I'm at the grocery store, standing in the produce aisle trying to pick out avocados, I'm just thinking about avocados. I'm trying to figure out which ones are ripe for tomorrow and which ones need a few days on the counter. My brain isn't suddenly, I don't know, conjuring up images of open blades while I'm looking at vegetables. Or if I'm at the gym, doing reps, I'm entirely focused on my form, my breathing, the audio in my headphones. I'm a big true crime podcast guy, actually, so I'm usually way too invested in whatever cold case they're talking about to let my mind wander off to grooming tools. I just keep myself busy, keep my mind occupied with normal, everyday stuff. 

I guess what I'm saying is, without a direct trigger—without someone mentioning work, or shaving, or me having to mentally prepare for my shift the next morning or text my boss about my schedule—the thought just doesn't materialize on its own. I don't just sit on my couch on a Tuesday night, completely relaxed, and spontaneously start picturing a straight razor and panicking. It just doesn't happen. If the context isn't there, the thought isn't there. My brain doesn't just randomly serve up that image to torture me while I'm waiting in line at the bank or something. So, yeah, no, I really can't think of any situation like that at all.
Is your fear of straight razors ever about something other than the potential harm they could cause to yourself or others?

No, it's really... it's entirely about the harm. The physical damage. It's not about, you know, germs or contamination or feeling like it's dirty, or even just a weird aesthetic aversion to the shape of it. It's 100% about the danger. 

And the crazy thing is, I know it's just a tool. I mean, I literally went to barbering school. I paid good money, spent hundreds of hours learning the trade, learning the anatomy of the face, the grain of the hair, the proper angle to hold the blade. I trained with these things. I know the mechanics of it. And I can use clippers all day long without batting an eye. I can use shears, trimmers, whatever. I can buzz a guy's head, edge him up, fade it out, totally fine. But the second it comes to the straight razor... when that thing is sitting open at my station, it's just a whole different ballgame. 

It just feels like... like this imminent catastrophe is just waiting to happen. Like I'm about to slip and hurt somebody, or cut myself badly. It's just this overwhelming, suffocating dread that blood is going to be drawn. Because, I mean, think about it—you're holding this incredibly sharp, completely unguarded piece of steel right against someone's jugular, or their cheek, or right by their eye. One tiny flinch, one sneeze, one microscopic slip of the wrist, and it's over. You've sliced them wide open. And that thought just loops in my head. The sheer potential for violence, even accidental violence, that's housed in that one little tool. So, yeah, it's never about anything else. It's just the pure, unadulterated fear of the physical harm it can cause.
If you were to see a straight razor in a completely neutral setting, like a museum or an antique shop, would you experience the same level of fear or anxiety as you do at work?

Yeah, I mean, I know we kind of touched on the museum thing a minute ago, but honestly, it would be the exact same reaction in an antique shop, too. Because it’s not a logical process, you know? It’s not like I look at it and weigh the pros and cons of the environment. It’s completely automatic. 

Like, if I’m at work, the absolute second I hear a client ask for the razor shave, or if I'm just wandering through some dusty antique shop looking at old pocket watches and suddenly I see a blade flipped open in one of those glass display cases... my body just reacts. Instantly. My chest tightens up so fast it's like someone pulled a strap around my ribs and I can't catch a full breath, and my hands get incredibly sweaty almost on command. 

And the craziest part is the physical instinct of it all. It’s literally like my body wants to back away before I even have time to think. Before my brain can even process, "oh, that's just an old vintage razor behind glass, it can't hurt me," my feet are already trying to step backward to put distance between me and the object. It's just this immediate, overwhelming physical response that hijacks my whole system. So, yeah, whether it’s a guy in my chair asking for a line-up or a random antique store on a Sunday afternoon, the second that blade is exposed, my body just goes into full reverse.
Do you think your fear of straight razors is something you've learned over time, possibly due to your experiences at work, or does it feel more like an innate reaction to you?

You know, that's... that's a really good question, actually. I've spent a lot of time thinking about that, trying to trace it back to some specific moment. Like, did I drop one in barbering school? Did I see someone else get cut? Did I watch a movie that just lodged in my subconscious? But... honestly, I don't know. I really don't. 

It's frustrating because I want there to be a reason. I want to be able to point to an event and say, "That's it, that's where it started," because then maybe I could fix it, right? Maybe I could unlearn it. But it doesn't feel like a learned thing. It feels more like... like a switch just flipped in my brain at some point. I mean, I used to practice with them when I first started learning the trade. I was nervous, sure, because it's a sharp blade and you're learning, but it was a normal kind of nervous. Respect for the tool, you know? 

But then, somewhere along the line, that normal respect just warped into this... this massive, uncontrollable terror. And I can't pinpoint a single incident at the shop, or with a client, or in my personal life that would justify it. It's just... it's like my brain suddenly decided, out of nowhere, that this specific object is the most dangerous thing in the world, and my body just goes along with it. So, I guess I'm not really sure if it's innate or learned, but it definitely doesn't feel tied to any logical experience I can actually remember. It just is.
Can you recall any situation where you felt anxious or afraid of straight razors when you were not at work and did not see one, but perhaps thought about it or heard it mentioned in a conversation?

You know, it's funny you ask that, because... well, not funny haha, but... I was just thinking about this the other day. Because you'd think, right? You'd think that if I'm not looking at one, if it's not sitting there on my station, gleaming under the fluorescent lights, or if I'm not in a situation where I might have to use one, that I'd be totally fine. And for the most part, I am. Like, if I'm just sitting at home watching TV or making dinner, I'm not just randomly paralyzed by the thought of a straight razor. 

But... and this is where it gets weird, and honestly, really exhausting... if someone brings it up, or if I see one in a movie or something... it's not like the full-blown panic attack I get when it's right in front of me, but it's definitely not nothing, either. 

Like, a couple of weeks ago, I was out getting a beer with some buddies from barbering school. We were just shooting the breeze, talking shop, complaining about difficult clients, you know, normal stuff. And one of them, Dave, he starts telling this story about a straight razor shave he did that day. He's going into all this detail about how the guy had this really tricky grain on his neck, and how he had to stretch the skin just right, and how the blade was catching a little bit... and I swear to you, just him talking about it... I could feel my heart rate start to pick up. 

It wasn't that immediate, overwhelming terror where I need to run away, but it was this... this really uncomfortable creeping sensation. Like my stomach just kind of dropped a little. I caught myself rubbing the back of my own neck, just imagining the blade there. And I had to change the subject. I just kind of awkwardly interrupted him and was like, "Hey, did you see the game last night?" because I could feel myself starting to spiral just visualizing the whole thing. 

Or, like, if I'm watching a movie... you know those old mob movies or Westerns where they always have the scene in the barbershop? The guy's sitting in the chair with the hot towel on his face, and the barber is stropping the razor... I can't watch it. I physically have to look away or leave the room. Even though I know it's a movie, even though I know it's fake blood or whatever, just the image of it, the sound of the blade on the strop... it just sets my teeth on edge. My palms get a little clammy, and I just feel this intense need to not be looking at it or thinking about it. 

So, yeah, it's not the same level of absolute panic as when it's right there in real life, but just the thought of it, or hearing someone describe using one... it definitely triggers something. It's like my brain just can't completely separate the idea of the razor from the actual physical threat of it, even if it's just a story or a scene on a screen. It's really frustrating, honestly, because it feels like I can't even escape it when I'm off the clock.
Can you think of any situation outside of work where the mere mention or thought of a straight razor, without actually seeing one, would cause you to feel anxious or afraid?

Well, yeah, I mean, like I was just saying with the story about Dave at the bar or watching those old movies... even just sitting here right now talking to you about it, which is obviously way outside of work, I can feel that anxiety bubbling up just from the mere thought of it. Because whenever someone mentions it, my brain immediately goes to the absolute worst-case scenario. 

It’s so incredibly frustrating because, intellectually, I know it’s just a tool I trained with. I went to school for this, I got my diploma, I put in all the required hours on the floor. And I can use clippers all day long—I can do skin fades, buzz cuts, intricate hard parts with the trimmers, and I don't even bat an eye. I'm completely relaxed, totally in my element. But the second my mind wanders to it, or if I actually picture it, or if I'm at work and that straight razor is sitting open at my station, it feels like I’m about to hurt somebody or cut myself badly. 

It’s like I can already see the accident happening in my head before I even pick the thing up. I just picture the blade slipping, or a client coughing or jerking their head at the wrong time, or me fumbling and dropping it and having it slice right through my shoe into my foot. Even though I'm sitting right here in your office, miles away from the barbershop, just visualizing it open on my rubber mat... it makes my chest tight all over again. I just can't shake that feeling of impending disaster, like the blade itself is just waiting for me to make a fatal mistake, you know? It doesn't matter where I am, if the thought pops into my head, it's just always that same terrifying image of it being open and exposed, and the absolute certainty that someone is going to end up bleeding.
Did something specific happen to you involving a straight razor that might have triggered this fear?

Well, see, that's the thing. Like I was kind of getting at earlier, I didn't slice someone's neck open, I didn't drop it and sever a tendon... it wasn't a bloody accident or anything like that. There wasn't one single catastrophic physical moment where the blade slipped. But... there was a specific situation. I guess you could call it a trigger, but it was more of a... a prolonged conflict, really. 

It all started about 11 months ago. The owner of the shop where I work—he's this guy who's always looking at the bottom line, always trying to find the next big up-sell to get more money out of the guys in the chair, you know how it is in this industry. Anyway, about 11 months ago, he decided we were going to roll out this new "premium grooming package." And the absolute centerpiece of this whole package, the thing he wanted us pushing on every single client who walked through the door, was a full, traditional, hot-towel straight-razor shave. 

Now, I pushed back on it immediately. Not because I was terrified of the razor at that exact moment, but because it’s a huge liability, it takes a ton of time to do it safely and correctly, and he wasn't adjusting our booking schedules to give us that extra time. He just expected us to squeeze a 30-minute service into a 15-minute window. So, we started arguing. And I mean, really going at it. He'd be on my case every single shift, pulling me into the back room, telling me I wasn't being a team player, demanding I start doing the straight-razor package or else. 

And it was right then, right when those arguments with the shop owner started getting really heated about 11 months ago, that this whole thing just... started. It was like all the stress, all the pressure, all the anger from fighting with him just got completely funneled into the razor itself. Every time I looked at it sitting on my station, I just felt all that intense pressure from management, and then that pressure just rapidly warped into this absolute, paralyzing fear of the blade. 

I mean, I've tried to explain to him that I literally cannot do it now, that my brain won't let me, but he just thinks I'm being stubborn about his business model. But it’s been 11 months of this absolute nightmare, just going in every day and dealing with this dread, and it all completely traces back to those stupid fights over that shave package.
Did you experience a traumatic event involving a straight razor before your fear started 11 months ago?

Well, no, honestly. And I've racked my brain trying to think if maybe I suppressed something, you know? Like maybe I nicked someone really bad back in barber school and just blocked it out, but... no. Nothing like that ever happened. Before 11 months ago, before all that drama with the shop owner and the premium packages started, the straight razor was literally just another piece of metal in my kit alongside my shears and clippers. 

I mean, I remember being in barber school, right? We had this whole extensive module just on traditional shaving. You start out shaving lather off balloons just to get the angle right—you have to hold the blade at exactly a 30-degree angle, keeping the tension on the balloon just like you would with real skin. If you mess up the angle or press too hard, the balloon pops and you get shaving cream absolutely everywhere. It's a whole rite of passage. But I was good at it! I barely ever popped the balloon, and I definitely never cut any of my classmates when we finally moved on to practicing on each other. It was just a normal, everyday part of the curriculum. 

I'd strop the blade, test the edge, do the hot towel prep... it was actually kind of relaxing back then, if you can believe it. It's an art form, really, a real classic barbering tradition. So, no, there was absolutely no trauma, no crazy blood-spurting accident, no close calls with a client's jugular or anything crazy like you'd see in a slasher movie. It was just totally, completely mundane. 

Which is exactly why this whole thing is so incredibly bizarre and frustrating to me now. Because it's like a switch just flipped in my brain 11 months ago during those heated arguments with my boss, and suddenly this tool I've handled a hundred times before without a single second thought became this... this terrifying, dangerous object. It makes zero sense to me. So yeah, before that 11-month mark, absolutely nothing traumatic happened. It was just normal, everyday barbering.
Did something specific happen to you involving a straight razor around the time your fear started 11 months ago?

Well, yeah, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really was just that whole conflict. There wasn't any specific physical accident with the razor itself right at that exact time, if that's what you're looking for. This whole thing has been going on for about 11 months, exactly since those arguments with the shop owner over the straight-razor shave package started. 

I mean, it's been a solid 11 months of this just... this heavy, exhausting cloud hanging over my station. If you really want to know what happened around that time, it was just the sheer volume and intensity of those fights. We were going at it constantly. I'd be sweeping up hair between cuts, or right in the middle of cashing out a client at the register, and he'd be hovering, hounding me about this premium package. He'd say things like, "Why aren't you upselling the shave? Why aren't you using the razor? You're leaving money on the table." And I'd be trying to explain the reality of the floor—the liability, the time crunch, the fact that you can't just rush a hot-towel shave in a 15-minute slot without risking someone's neck. But he wouldn't hear it. 

So it just escalated and escalated. And for the past 11 months, every single day I walk into that shop, I'm not just looking at a tool on my mat, you know? I'm looking at 11 months of non-stop tension, 11 months of my boss breathing down my neck, 11 months of feeling like my job is on the line because I won't do this one specific service. And for the most part, I am. Like, if I'm just sitting at home watching TV or making dinner, I'm not just randomly paralyzed by the thought of a straight razor. 

But... and this is where it gets weird, and honestly, really exhausting... if someone brings it up, or if I see one in a movie or something... it's not like the full-blown panic attack I get when it's right in front of me, but it's definitely not nothing, either. 

Like, a couple of weeks ago, I was out getting a beer with some buddies from barbering school. We were just shooting the breeze, talking shop, complaining about difficult clients, you know, normal stuff. And one of them, Dave, he starts telling this story about a straight razor shave he did that day. He's going into all this detail about how the guy had this really tricky grain on his neck, and how he had to stretch the skin just right, and how the blade was catching a little bit... and I swear to you, just him talking about it... I could feel my heart rate start to pick up. 

It wasn't that immediate, overwhelming terror where I need to run away, but it was this... this really uncomfortable creeping sensation. Like my stomach just kind of dropped a little. I caught myself rubbing the back of my own neck, just imagining the blade there. And I had to change the subject. I just kind of awkwardly interrupted him and was like, "Hey, did you see the game last night?" because I could feel myself starting to spiral just visualizing the whole thing. 

Or, like, if I'm watching a movie... you know those old mob movies or Westerns where they always have the scene in the barbershop? The guy's sitting in the chair with the hot towel on his face, and the barber is stropping the razor... I can't watch it. I physically have to look away or leave the room. Even though I know it's a movie, even though I know it's fake blood or whatever, just the image of it, the sound of the blade on the strop... it just sets my teeth on edge. My palms get a little clammy, and I just feel this intense need to not be looking at it or thinking about it. 

So, yeah, it's not the same level of absolute panic as when it's right there in real life, but just the thought of it, or hearing someone describe using one... it definitely triggers something. It's like my brain just can't completely separate the idea of the razor from the actual physical threat of it, even if it's just a story or a scene on a screen. It's really frustrating, honestly, because it feels like I can't even escape it when I'm off the clock.

And I can use clippers all day long—I can do skin fades, buzz cuts, intricate hard parts with the trimmers, and I don't even bat an eye. I'm completely relaxed, totally in my element. But the second my mind wanders to it, or if I actually picture it, or if I'm at work and that straight razor is sitting open at my station, it feels like I’m about to hurt somebody or cut myself badly. 

It’s like I can already see the accident happening in my head before I even pick the thing up. I just picture the blade slipping, or a client coughing or jerking their head at the wrong time, or me fumbling and dropping it and having it slice right through my shoe into my foot. Even though I'm sitting right here in your office, miles away from the barbershop, just visualizing it open on my rubber mat... it makes my chest tight all over again. I just can't shake that feeling of impending disaster, like the blade itself is just waiting for me to make a fatal mistake, you know? It doesn't matter where I am, if the thought pops into my head, it's just always that same terrifying image of it being open and exposed, and the absolute certainty that someone is going to end up bleeding.

Well, see, that's the thing. Like I was kind of getting at earlier, I didn't slice someone's neck open, I didn't drop it and sever a tendon... it wasn't a bloody accident or anything like that. There wasn't one single catastrophic physical moment where the blade slipped. But... there was a specific situation. I guess you could call it a trigger, but it was more of a... a prolonged conflict, really. 

It all started about 11 months ago. The owner of the shop where I work—he's this guy who's always looking at the bottom line, always trying to find the next big up-sell to get more money out of the guys in the chair, you know how it is in this industry. Anyway, about 11 months ago, he decided we were going to roll out this new "premium grooming package." And the absolute centerpiece of this whole package, the thing he wanted us pushing on every single client who walked through the door, was a full, traditional, hot-towel straight-razor shave. 

Now, I pushed back on it immediately. Not because I was terrified of the razor at that exact moment, but because it’s a huge liability, it takes a ton of time to do it safely and correctly, and he wasn't adjusting our booking schedules to give us that extra time. He just expected us to squeeze a 30-minute service into a 15-minute window. So, we started arguing. And I mean, really going at it. He'd be on my case every single shift, pulling me into the back room, telling me I wasn't being a team player, demanding I start doing the straight-razor package or else. 

And it was right then, right when those arguments with the shop owner started getting really heated about 11 months ago, that this whole thing just... started. It was like all the stress, all the pressure, all the anger from fighting with him just got completely funneled into the razor itself. Every time I looked at it sitting on my station, I just felt all that intense pressure from management, and then that pressure just rapidly warped into this absolute, paralyzing fear of the blade. 

I mean, I've tried to explain to him that I literally cannot do it now, that my brain won't let me, but he just thinks I'm being stubborn about his business model. But it’s been 11 months of this absolute nightmare, just going in every day and dealing with this dread, and it all completely traces back to those stupid fights over that shave package.

You start out shaving lather off balloons just to get the angle right—you have to hold the blade at exactly a 30-degree angle, keeping the tension on the balloon just like you would with real skin. If you mess up the angle or press too hard, the balloon pops and you get shaving cream absolutely everywhere. It's a whole rite of passage. But I was good at it! I barely ever popped the balloon, and I definitely never cut any of my classmates when we finally moved on to practicing on each other. It was just a normal, everyday part of the curriculum. 

I'd strop the blade, test the edge, do the hot towel prep... it was actually kind of relaxing back then, if you can believe it. It's an art form, really, a real classic barbering tradition. So, no, there was absolutely no trauma, no crazy blood-spurting accident, no close calls with a client's jugular or anything crazy like you'd see in a slasher movie. It was just totally, completely mundane. 

Which is exactly why this whole thing is so incredibly bizarre and frustrating to me now. Because it's like a switch just flipped in my brain 11 months ago during those heated arguments with my boss, and suddenly this tool I've handled a hundred times before without a single second thought became this... this terrifying, dangerous object. It makes zero sense to me. So yeah, before that 11-month mark, absolutely nothing traumatic happened. It was just normal, everyday barbering.
